title: The cost of a free opportunity.
description: Why a zero price does not mean a choice costs nothing.
author: OpenEconomics
caption: CHOICES HAVE CONTEXT.

sections.title: A price is only part of the decision.
paragraphs: Imagine a student choosing between a free economics workshop and a paid shift. The workshop has no admission charge, but attending still uses two hours. If working is the student’s next-best alternative, the value of that shift is the opportunity cost of attending.

Economists use opportunity cost to describe the value of the next-best alternative forgone. The idea applies to time, land, attention and public resources as well as money. A zero price removes one possible expense; it does not remove scarcity.

sections.title: Choose the next-best alternative.
paragraphs: Suppose the student could work, revise for an exam or meet a friend. Opportunity cost does not add together all three alternatives. Only one could have occupied the same time. The relevant comparison is the best alternative the student would actually give up.

That value may include more than wages. The student might value revision or time with a friend more highly. Identifying the next-best alternative requires understanding the person’s circumstances and preferences.

sections.title: The same question matters for institutions.
paragraphs: A library that already owns a meeting room may offer it to a learning group without charging rent. Yet using the room still has an opportunity cost if another valuable activity could have taken place there. If the room would otherwise have stood empty, the alternative use may have little value. Context matters.

This does not mean every free program should charge a fee. It means a useful evaluation asks what participants and institutions give up, alongside what they gain. Travel, timing and access to a device can all affect whether an opportunity is practical.

sections.title: A better question to ask.
paragraphs: Instead of asking only “Is this free?”, ask “What would I otherwise do with these resources?” Then compare the expected benefits of the available choices. A worthwhile workshop can have an opportunity cost and still be the best choice.
Understanding a trade-off is a starting point for a decision. It does not determine the decision on its own.

title: Local knowledge brings better questions.
description: A perspective on why community voices belong in educational design.
author: OpenEconomics
caption: PERSPECTIVE OPENS POSSIBILITY.

sections.title: Start by asking, not assuming.
paragraphs: A learning resource can be available online and still be difficult to use. Language, curriculum expectations, schedules and access to devices can affect what a learner needs. A useful starting point is to ask people in the community how learning already happens.

sections.title: Relationships can reveal the practical details.
paragraphs: The ambassador approach gives local contributors a role in listening to learners, introducing institutions and gathering feedback. A conversation with an educator may identify a need for a printable explanation. A library may be better placed to host a discussion than an individual student is to organize one.
Working with the people who use a resource helps keep the format practical and relevant.

sections.title: Make feedback part of the work.
paragraphs: Local participation should influence decisions, not simply distribute a finished resource. Useful feedback describes which examples made sense, where an explanation became difficult, and what practical barriers remained.
Community voices help us understand how resources are used and where educational needs remain.

title: Building more ways to learn.
description: The direction behind the academy, community programs and institutional access.
author: OpenEconomics
caption: ONE PURPOSE. MANY PATHWAYS.

sections.title: One mission, several routes.
paragraphs: OpenEconomics brings digital learning together with publications, library access, educational partnerships and local leadership. Each route addresses a different part of the same question: how can more people find, understand and use economic knowledge?

sections.title: Learning on the screen, and beyond it.
paragraphs: OEP Learn brings together courses, questions and tools for exploring economics. Workshops, essay competitions and learning circles create additional formats for discussion, application and feedback.
Digital resources, community learning and institutional collaboration offer different ways to make economics accessible.

sections.title: What future updates should show.
paragraphs: An organizational update should explain what changed, who it serves and what evidence supports the account. When an activity has taken place, the story can include approved participant voices, the materials used, dates and documented outcomes.
Follow OEP for updates on educational resources, community programs and opportunities to take part.
